## ABSTRACT

The U.S. dollar appreciates in the run-up to foreign exchange (FX) fixes and depreciates thereafter, tracing a W-shaped return pattern around the clock. Return reversals for the top nine traded currencies over a 21-year period are pervasive and highly statistically significant, and they imply daily swings of more than one billion U.S. dollars based on spot volumes. Using natural experiments, we document the existence of a published reference rate determines the timing of intraday return reversals.
We present evidence consistent with an inventory risk explanation whereby FX dealers intermediate unconditional demand for U.S. dollars at the fixes.

The foreign exchange (FX) market trades continuously on a 24-hour, decentralized basis across the globe in different time zones. Every day, benchmark rates are determined using specific procedures and published at preset times. These currency fixes are well established and widely followed, yet there exists surprisingly little understanding of how they affect (intraday) price formation.

In this paper, we study high-frequency currency returns around the clock and document a novel intraday return pattern: the U.S. dollar gradually appreciates against all currencies ahead of the three major currency fixes in Tokyo, Frankfurt (the European Central Bank (ECB) fix) and London, and reverts thereafter.

To establish this fact, we compute intraday returns from January 1999 to December 2019 for the G9 currency pairs, which cover roughly 75% of daily spot turnover (see, e.g., BIS (【16†2019】)). Consider the dollar portfolio that invests in foreign currencies against the U.S. dollar. On average, this portfolio depreciates by approximately 2 basis points (bps) in the run-up to the Tokyo and European fixes and appreciates by the same magnitude during the postfix period.

In particular, during Asian or European trading hours, the U.S. dollar remains flat on average but displays two V-shaped return reversals with turning points marked by the fixes that take place at 9:55 Tokyo time, 14:15 Frankfurt time, and 16:00 London time.

The price patterns that we detect are highly pervasive and, given the size of the spot market alone, economically meaningful. Based on daily turnover from the 2019 Bank for International Settlements (BIS) Triennial Survey, the patterns that we detect imply swings exceeding one billion U.S. dollars per day. In statistical terms, the average fluctuations in the dollar portfolio during the respective windows are highly significant with t-statistics ranging between 4.5 and 11.7.

Moreover, patterns for the dollar portfolio continue to hold across individual currency pairs with a large degree of statistical confidence. All G9 currencies display V-shaped reversal patterns around the Tokyo and European fixes, except for the yen, which depreciates after the London fix.

To study the persistence of fix reversals, we calculate returns to a strategy that goes long the U.S. dollar before the fix and reverses the position thereafter. Ignoring transaction costs, these reversal returns are consistently positive and large. Around the Tokyo fix, an initial position of one U.S. dollar in 1999 grows to 12, 9, and 5 U.S. dollars by 2019 for the yen, euro, and dollar portfolio, respectively. Around the European fixes (going long the U.S. dollar before the ECB fix and short the U.S.
dollar after the London fix), the initial position grows to 27, 14, and 6 U.S. dollars for the euro, pound, and dollar portfolio, respectively.

To show that the fixes are the salient turning points within the day, we calculate alternative reversal returns for both the Tokyo and European windows. We find that the returns are indeed maximized exactly when the reversal points are aligned with the fixing times and not when equity markets open or economic news is released.

Providing additional evidence pinning down turning points within the day, we conduct a series of natural experiments. We begin by exploiting the fact that Japan does not follow Daylight Saving Time (DST). This means that the time difference between New York and Tokyo varies between 14 hours during winter and 13 hours when DST is observed from March to November. Measured in Eastern Time (ET), the peak of the U.S. dollar around the Tokyo fix shifts by exactly one hour when DST is observed.
By contrast, there is no change in the timing of the reversals around the European fixes.

Next, because holidays are nonsynchronous across countries, we have 304 Japanese holidays in our sample for which reference rates are not published for the Tokyo fix (see also Ito and Yamada (【17†2017】)). Thus, if reversals are tied to the existence of a fix, they should not emerge on Japanese holidays that are normal trading days in other countries.
Indeed, we find no significant return patterns around the Tokyo fix on these days, while the reversals around the European fixes remain high and statistically significant.

Conducting a third natural experiment, we extend our data set to investigate price patterns starting in 1986, before the introduction of the London and the ECB fixes in 1994 and 1999, respectively. Return patterns look distinctly different before the introduction of the fixes, and the turning points we document emerge only after the published reference rates become recognized as established benchmarks.

This result is also reflected in trading quantities over time, with the fixes becoming increasingly relevant, consistent with theories of “liquidity begets liquidity” (see, e.g., Duffie, Dworczak, and Zhu (【18†2017】)). We estimate that during our main sample period, between 30% and 40% of traded volume is executed during the three hours leading up to the London fix and the hour thereafter.

Taken together, nonsynchronous holidays and intraday patterns in the prefix era demonstrate the novelty of our contribution: when the fixes are not published (including when they do not exist), reversals do not occur; when they are published, we observe reversals.

Moving beyond the empirical characteristics of fix return reversals, we look to the market microstructure literature for an economic explanation. Broadly speaking, this literature offers two explanations: (i) asymmetric information and (ii) inventory management. For asymmetric information alone to explain a systematic appreciation of the U.S. dollar, news to informed traders should be systematically revealed before the fix and this information should be positive for the U.S. dollar on average.

However, we show that standard information releases, such as an international cross section of macroeconomic and monetary policy announcements, do not explain fix reversals, suggesting that asymmetric information alone is an implausible explanation.【19†1】 The second strand of the literature recognizes that in supplying liquidity, financial intermediaries face inventory risk for which they demand a premium.

The effects on prices following supply and demand shocks in such a setting are well understood and known to be transient. Thus, standard models of inventory management do predict price reversals.【20†2】

Accordingly, using data from the Refinitiv FX Matching (RM) interdealer platform for the period 2006 to 2019, we study an inventory management explanation. As RM is the dominant platform for Commonwealth currencies, we focus on the Australian dollar (AUD) and the British pound (GBP). Moreover, we follow existing literature and use order imbalances in the dealer-to-dealer (D2D) market to proxy for aggregate order imbalances in the dealer-to-client (D2C) market.

First, we show that the unconditional return patterns correspond with unconditional order imbalances in the dealer market toward an excess demand for U.S. dollars in the hours before and at the fixes. For example, the median order imbalance tilted toward U.S. dollar demand (DD) before the London fix on RM for both the AUD and the GBP is around 20 million U.S. dollars.
Prefix order imbalances are statistically significant and economically large, translating to around 6% of volume traded ahead of the London fix.

Second, we document that returns for providing immediacy are related to the size of the order imbalance and to uncertainty as measured by volatility in the FX market. Using double sorts on order imbalance and intraday FX volatility (FXV), we find that return reversals are (i) not only in line with the direction but also monotonically increasing in the conditional order imbalance, and (ii) larger during periods of high uncertainty.
For example, in states of high DD, reversal returns go from 16 to 30 bps and from 22 to 29 bps for the AUD and the GBP, respectively, as we move from low- to high-volatility states.

Third, we explore returns to liquidity provision. We consider a hypothetical scenario with a dealer that understands there is unconditional demand for U.S. dollars and builds up U.S. dollar inventory acting as a liquidity provider. We also consider a trader who does not have access to the dealer market, but trades to exploit the V-shaped return pattern around the European fixes.

We show that the unconditional return patterns cannot easily be arbitraged in the client market as transaction cost-adjusted returns are significantly negative. At the same time, returns to liquidity provision are positive and strongly statistically significant, as is the difference between the liquidity-demanding and the liquidity-supplying trade. Overall, our findings are consistent with the idea that clients are demanding U.S.
dollars at the fixes and dealers are gradually raising their prices when streaming quotes to clients, thereby supplying U.S. dollars in exchange for a liquidity premium.

In summary, we present evidence consistent with an inventory risk explanation and show that there is unconditional demand for U.S. dollars at the fixes. However, while unconditional demand for U.S. dollars is consistent with an unconditional V-shaped reversal pattern, our analysis is silent with regards to the origins of this imbalance. We speculate that predictable demand for U.S. dollars at the fix is related to the special role of the United States as the world's provider of safe assets and the U.S.
dollar as the world's reserve currency.

Related Literature: The intraday price patterns documented in this paper are related to a well-established literature on intraday FX patterns starting with Wasserfallen (【21†1989】) and Cornett, Schwarz, and Szakmary (【22†1995】) and followed more recently, by Ranaldo (【23†2009】) and Breedon and Ranaldo (【24†2013】), who document that local currencies depreciate during local working hours.
With respect to these papers, our granular dissection allows us to identify price reversals around major currency fixes that are not explained by working hours patterns.

Our paper is also related to a literature in market microstructure on FX benchmarks. For the London fix, Melvin and Prins (【25†2015】) analyze hedging flows of fund managers at month-end, Evans (【26†2018】) assesses price dynamics in tight windows around the fix, while Evans et al. (【27†2020】) document differences in trading behavior across investor types. Ito and Yamada (【28†2016】) document a structural demand for U.S. dollars at the Tokyo fix. Different from these papers, we show that U.S.
DD systematically manifests at both the Tokyo and the European fixes, leading to a gradual appreciation and depreciation of the U.S. dollar that traces out a W-shaped return pattern around the clock.
## I. FX Benchmarks

An FX fix is a preset time of day when bids and offers are aggregated and a reference price is published. Historically, the most popular fixes are the London, ECB, and Tokyo fixes. Figure 【29†1】 depicts these fixes visually in ET (the time in New York) “around the clock.” The colored blocks in Figure 【29†1】 show the regular trading hours in the futures markets of each location.

The figure begins at 17:00 ET, which is the end of the trading day in New York and roughly the beginning of the trading day in Australasia.【30†3】 The first major currency fix that occurs is Tokyo at 9:55 local time, or 20:55 ET (19:55 ET when DST is not in effect in the United States). The red, green, and yellow blocks overlap, meaning that as Japanese trading is closing, European markets are opening.

While the beginning of the trading day in New York (we assume 8:00 ET) is close to the ECB fix at 8:15 ET (14:15 local time), the timing is clearly not exactly aligned. Moreover, and importantly, the ECB fix is also not aligned with the typical release time of macro announcements, at 8:30 ET. As we argue below, this distinction in timing is important when considering intraday price movements in exchange rates. The final and most important fix of the day is the London fix at 16:00 local time (11:00 ET).

While all fixes affect FX markets, they differ from each other with respect to institutional characteristics, reference rate publication times, and methodologies used to compute fix rates.

First, the Tokyo fix rates are published at 10:00 local time, with each bank determining its own individual fix rate for their customers. This is a major difference compared to the ECB and London fixes, where only one reference rate is published. The rates of the Tokyo fix are based on transacted prices, which banks sample from their own customer transactions at exactly 9:55. Furthermore, the fix rate applies to not only prefix but also postfix customer orders, which are submitted after 10:00.
The Tokyo fix rate, therefore, has far-reaching consequences for banks over the remainder of the trading day (see, e.g., Ito and Yamada (【28†2016】)).

Second, reference rates from the ECB fix are based on a daily teleconference between eurozone central banks at 14:15 Central European Time (CET). The reference rates are the average of quoted bid and offer prices against the euro, which means that the ECB reference rate is not based on actual transactions. However, the ECB reference rates are often used by nonfinancial corporations in the euro area that use forward contracts for hedging purposes (see, e.g., FSB (【33†2014】)).

To emphasize that the euro FX reference rates are for information purposes only, and to discourage use of the ECB fix for transactions, the ECB has moved the publication of the reference rates to 16:00 CET in July 2016 while keeping the methodology unchanged (ECB (【34†2019】)). In direct response, Thomson Reuters launched the WM/Reuters 14:00 CET benchmark to target corporates that had previously valued, hedged, and settled cross-border transactions using the ECB fix.

Finally, the WM/Reuters London fix rate is set at 16:00 London time and published by Thomson Reuters. The benchmark rates are computed based on trades (and quotes for less-liquid currency pairs) in a window around 16:00.

In a five-minute interval around the fix (i.e., between 15:57:30 and 16:02:30), traded rates are sourced every second from major FX platforms and a median trade based on bid and offer rates is calculated from the pooled sample of trades.【35†4】 In contrast to the Tokyo fix, the London fix applies only to orders that arrive before 16:00 local time and that are requested to execute at the benchmark rate.
The London fix is prominently used by various groups of market participants to value their international portfolio positions (see, e.g., Melvin and Prins (【25†2015】)).
## II. Data
Our data come from multiple sources including Refinitiv Tick History (RTH), RM, Chicago Mercantile Exchange (CME), Intercontinental Exchange (ICE), and Olsen Financial Technologies.

In this section, we briefly describe the main data; we discuss additional data sources and further details regarding data preprocessing and cleaning in Section 【36†I】 in the 【37†Internet Appendix】.【38†5】 Our full sample starts in January 1999 and ends in December 2019, covering 21 years of high-frequency, tick-by-tick data for the G9 currencies, including the AUD, the Canadian dollar (CAD), the euro (EUR), the Japanese yen (JPY), the New Zealand dollar (NZD), the Norwegian krone (NOK), the Swedish krona (SEK), the Swiss franc (CHF), and the GBP, all vis-à-vis the U.S.

dollar. These currencies are the most liquid currencies over the sample period, and together they account for close to 75% of total daily turnover in the FX market based on calculations using information available from the latest BIS Triennial Survey (see BIS (【16†2019】)).

For the period January 1999 to December 2019, we obtain high-frequency indicative bid and ask quotes from RTH, which aggregates quotes from individual banks that are available to market participants to trade “bank-to-client.” From the RTH data, we cannot gauge the volume of transactions or the price at which transactions are executed even though most transactions in the FX market are still executed over-the-counter.

Starting in June 2006, we also have real-time data from the RM platform on traded prices as well as volumes. Furthermore, the RM data include information that allows us to calculate various measures of order flow. Together with Electronic Broking Services (EBS), RM is the leading interdealer platform for FX trading, with daily volume for spot transactions exceeding 100 billion U.S. dollars (compared to around 76 billion U.S. dollars traded on EBS).

While not all currency pairs are equally liquid on both platforms (e.g., RM is the leading platform for Commonwealth currencies), Breedon and Vitale (【39†2010】) show that returns for a given currency pair are highly correlated.
## III. Currency Returns around the Clock

In this section, we provide novel evidence on the intraday behavior of currency returns. In particular, we document the following novel stylized fact: exchange rate returns display predictable intraday seasonality, with the U.S. dollar appreciating in the run-up to FX fixes and depreciating thereafter.
### A. Dissecting Currency Returns

Denote by $$s_{t}$$ the log of the exchange rate, expressed in units of U.S. dollar per foreign currency, and $$\Delta s_{t}$$ the change in the log exchange rate between time $$t-1$$ and t. A negative $$\Delta s_{t}$$ corresponds to appreciation of the U.S. dollar relative to the foreign currency. Working in ET, we define daily close-to-close log spot returns ($$\Delta s_t^{\text{CTC}}$$) as the percent change in the mid-quote from 17:00 on day $$t-1$$ to 17:00 on day t,
$$$$\begin{align} \Delta s_t^{\text{CTC}} = s^{17:00}_t - s^{17:00}_{t-1}. \end{align}$$$$(1)

Next, we split the day into different periods guided by the timing of the three main currency fixes across the globe, namely, the Tokyo fix at 9:55 local time, the ECB fix at 14:15 local time, and the London fix at 16:00 local time.

Accordingly, we calculate returns for the following five intraday windows (all times expressed in ET): (i) pre-Tokyo fix (“pre-T,” 17:00 to 20:55), (ii) post-Tokyo fix (“post-T,” 20:55 to 2:00), (iii) pre-ECB fix (“pre-E,” 2:00 to 8:15), (iv) ECB fix to London fix (“E-L,” 8:15 to 11:00), and (v) post-London fix (“post-L,” 11:00 to 17:00).【40†6】 To distinguish between the post-Tokyo and the pre-ECB fix periods, we use 8:00 Frankfurt time (2:00 ET), that is, the beginning of the FX trading day in Europe.
Similarly, we define the start of the FX trading day in New York as 8:00 ET.

All currencies show a distinct pattern of depreciation against the U.S. dollar ahead of the Tokyo fix at 20:55 ET followed by a reversal thereafter. Once European markets open at 2:00 ET, all currencies depreciate against the U.S. dollar ahead of the ECB fix. This drop is stronger for the European currencies and more muted for the AUD, NZD, and CAD.

The period between the ECB and London fix does not exhibit a clear pattern in the cross section aside from the EUR and JPY, which appreciate until one hour before the London fix. After the London fix, all currencies show a strong appreciation versus the U.S. dollar. This continues until the end of the business day in the U.S. at 17:00 ET, with the JPY being the sole exception moving in the opposite direction. Overall, all currencies apart from the JPY appreciate during the U.S.
intraday period and depreciate overnight.【45†7】

Aggregating across currencies, the consistent depreciation of foreign currencies before the Tokyo fix and after European markets open combined with the depreciation of the U.S. dollar during the intraday period leads to a distinctive W-shaped pattern of cumulative returns measured over a full day.

On average, the intraday appreciation and depreciation of the U.S. dollar amounts to around 2 bps twice a day. Given the size of the FX spot market, this translates into very large sums. Using daily turnover numbers from the 2019 BIS Triennial Survey, the pattern we detect implies daily swings exceeding one billion U.S. dollars.

As noted above, all foreign currencies depreciate against the U.S. dollar after trading in New York ceases and in anticipation of the Tokyo fix. The AUD and NZD (−2.8 and −3.4 bps, respectively) show the most negative average returns, while the CHF and the CAD depreciate the least compared to other currency pairs. Average returns of all currency pairs differ from zero at the 1% level of significance.

The reversal after the Tokyo fix is equally statistically significant for all currencies in our sample, with the JPY and the NOK exhibiting the highest magnitudes of 3.0 and 3.2 bps per day, respectively. Not surprisingly, the DOL exhibits a strong and significant reversal pattern as well, dropping around 2 bps per day before the Tokyo fix and recouping the losses thereafter.

Leading up to the ECB fix, the European currencies and the yen depreciate significantly against the U.S. dollar. The point estimates are measured with a large degree of statistical confidence. The greatest drops are observed for the EUR and the SEK, of −3.5 and −3.1 bps per day, respectively. Between the ECB and the London fixes, currencies do not move as consistently in the cross section as during other windows.
This may be because the window contains both a post-ECB fix depreciation and a pre-London fix appreciation of the U.S. dollar as can be seen in Figures 【41†2】 and 【42†3】.

After the London fix, the pattern is again quite striking: with the exception of the yen, all currencies appreciate strongly (i.e., between 1.5 bps for the CAD and 2.7 bps for the EUR) during the period between the London fix and the close of markets in the United States, whereas the JPY depreciates by 1.2 bps. Overall, the DOL appreciates by 1.8 bps and movements for all currencies are strongly statistically significant.

The last column in Table 【46†I】 makes clear that the pattern we document represents intraday seasonality (i.e., a predictable component) that does not carry over to close-to-close returns. In fact, none of the currencies in our sample moves by more than 1 bp per day over our sample period and none of the close-to-close returns is statistically significant.
### C. Robustness
We study the robustness of the reversals around the fixes along two dimensions: (i) over time and (ii) across data sets.

Table 【49†II】 splits intraday DOL returns for the respective windows into four subsamples. In each subsample, we observe a W-shaped return pattern across the 24-hour trading day. The reversal of the DOL is strongly significant in all subsamples between 1999 and 2014, averaging around 2 bps per day on either side of the fix. In the 2014 to 2019 sample, the reversal around the Tokyo fix is notably smaller but remains statistically significant.

Thus, pre- and postfix returns are strongly robust over time and consistent with a reversal that nets out to zero on average, implying that intraday FX seasonalities are a robust feature of daily data. That said, on a daily basis the movements remain on the order of a few bps, which begs the question of whether the pattern is merely an artifact of using RTH indicative quotes to calculate log spot changes.

In summary, the central contribution of this paper—the observation that the U.S. dollar appreciates in the run-up to FX fixes and depreciates thereafter—is robust over time, across data sets, and across different segments of the FX market. This finding is important for a number of reasons that go beyond pure academic interest.

Most importantly, the presence of robust intraday seasonality in FX spot and derivatives markets implies that the timing of portfolio adjustments should be an important consideration for asset managers, institutional investors, and corporates who receive cash flows in U.S. dollars and must convert back to their local currencies, or vice versa.
## IV. Reversal Returns

In this section, we study a trading strategy that exploits the reversals by taking a long position in the U.S. dollar before the Tokyo and ECB fixes, that is, reversed post-Tokyo and post-London fix, respectively:

$$$$\begin{equation} \Delta s_t^{\text{Tokyo}} = -\Delta s_t^{\text{pre-T}} +\Delta s_t^{\text{post-T}} \quad \text{and} \quad \Delta s_t^{\text{Europe}} = -\Delta s_t^{\text{pre-E}} +\Delta s_t^{\text{post-L}}, \end{equation}$$$$(2)

where $$\Delta s_t^{\text{pre-T}}$$ and $$\Delta s_t^{\text{post-T}}$$ are the returns for the pre- and post-Tokyo windows, and $$s_t^{\text{pre-E}}$$ and $$\Delta s_t^{\text{post-L}}$$ are the returns for the pre-ECB and the post-London windows, respectively. Note that the reversal returns are defined for either the Tokyo or the Europe window.
The latter does not include the interval between the ECB and the London fixes, as the results in Table 【46†I】 suggest that there is no clear directional movement during that period.

## V. Natural Experiments

This section further highlights the importance of the fixes in pinning down intraday reversals using three quasi-natural experiments that exploit (i) the fact that Japan does not follow DST, (ii) asynchronous holidays between Japan and the United States, and (iii) data before and after the introduction of the London and ECB fixes in 1994 and 1999, respectively.
### A. A DST Test

Because Japan does not follow DST, the time difference between New York and Tokyo varies throughout the year: it is 14 hours during the winter but an hour less when DST is observed between March and November. In Figure 【61†6】, we plot the intraday patterns for the EUR, GBP, and JPY during Japanese trading hours but aligned with ET (i.e., New York time). The results clearly show that the spike in the U.S. dollar at the Tokyo fix moves by one hour during roughly eight months of the year (from the perspective of a U.S. investor). At the same time, no clear pattern emerges that could be attributed to the start or the end of the business day. This means that while a clear shift in the spike of the price pattern aligns with the Tokyo fix, no comparable differences exist for the equivalent move of Asian market opening and closing times measured in ET.

## VI. Order Imbalances and Price Reversals

In this section, we argue that the FX market microstructure literature provides a potential economic explanation for the return patterns we document. Broadly speaking, this literature offers two explanations for intraday price patterns: (i) the presence of asymmetric information in the market, and (ii) inventory (risk) management by market makers.

The latter strand of the literature recognizes that in supplying liquidity, financial intermediaries (arbitrageurs) face inventory risk for which they demand a premium. The premium demanded by liquidity providers arises through bid-ask spreads and through positive expected returns for holding risky assets. Supply and demand shocks have a transient impact and generate price reversals in such a setting.

We show that our main empirical finding is consistent with an explanation based on demand for immediacy combined with a structural demand for U.S. dollars at the fixes. In Section 【72†III】 of the 【37†Internet Appendix】, we discuss and rule out a set of alternative potential explanations, such as news about the macroeconomy and monetary policy, suggesting that (asymmetric) information alone is an implausible explanation for the intraday return patterns we document.
Moreover, the patterns are not explained by intraday volatility, price jumps, or variation in market liquidity.
### A. Inventory Management

In benchmark models of inventory management (see, e.g., Stoll (【73†1978】), and Grossman and Miller (【74†1988】)), dealers provide liquidity to traders who demand immediacy before offsetting their positions to new traders arriving later in the day. A feature of these models is that prices exhibit reversal patterns around “liquidity events” due to order imbalances absorbed by intermediaries.
We argue that the key times within the day for liquidity events to occur, that is, for order imbalances to manifest, are at the major fixings.

To support this claim, we study D2D trading volumes on RM, the leading interdealer platform for Commonwealth currencies. Figure 【75†9】 depicts trading volumes throughout the day for the G9 currencies.【76†14】 For every hour over a 24-hour period, we calculate the average fraction of daily volume traded. For all currencies, the two hours around the London fix are the busiest with a total fraction of between 17.5% and 27% traded, while the second busiest hours are those around the ECB fix.

Even though trading on RM is concentrated during European and U.S. trading hours in general, the heatmap also reveals a spike in trading activity around the Tokyo fix for the JPY, the AUD, and the NZD.

We start by examining the relationship between the unconditional reversal patterns and unconditional order imbalances. Grossman and Miller (【74†1988】) write that “in the absence of an asynchronization of order flows [reversal returns should equal zero]. The explanation proposed in this section relies on structural demand for U.S. dollars arising in the D2C market. However, our order flow data are available only for a D2D platform. When inferring structural demand for U.S. dollars from our data, we assume that D2D order flow can act as a proxy for D2C order flow.

This is in line with a large literature (see, e.g., Evans and Lyons (【86†2002】), Ito and Yamada (【17†2017】), or Bjønnes, Osler, and Rime (【87†2021】)) that tests inventory and asymmetric information models in which D2D order flow is predicted to have explanatory power for contemporaneous and leading price changes. Indeed, the two-tier structure of the FX market is such that a vast majority of volume is intermediated by a small number of liquidity providers.

Put differently, a small number of dealers absorb order flow from a vast number of customers.【88†19】 Managing inventory risk, these dealers try to internally offset dollar supply or demand as much as possible by dealing with customers directly. Remaining imbalances that cannot be hedged internally are routed to interdealer platforms and offloaded to other liquidity traders.

Thus, any demand imbalance observable in the D2D market can be reasonably assumed to be positively correlated with unobservable aggregate imbalances arising in the D2C market. Moreover, these imbalances drive inventory effects with risk-averse market makers.
### C. Conditional Order Imbalance and FXV

To this end, we double sort the daily reversal returns defined in Section 【63†IV】 for the Europe window into six portfolios based on prefix net DD (low, medium, and high) and FXV (low, high). We use the same definition for order flow as above, implying that low net DD is characterized by positive order flow and high net DD by negative order flow. FXV is computed as the intraday sum of squared returns during the previous day computed at the one-minute sampling frequency.

That is, there is no tendency of prefix DD to arise in states of larger FXV or vice versa. In terms of economic magnitudes, return reversals can be quite large depending on whether volatility is high or low. For DD^{L}, the reversal returns go from −15 to −25 bps for the AUD and from −12 to −24 bps for the GBP; for DD^{H}, the reversal returns increase from 16 to 30 bps for the AUD and from 22 to 29 bps for the GBP. In sum, as predicted by Grossman and Miller (【74†1988】)-style models, return reversals are larger in magnitude when order imbalances are larger in absolute terms, and even more so in periods of heightened uncertainty as proxied by FXV.
### D. Asymmetric Information versus Inventory Effects

We now study a regression specification closely related to Campbell, Grossman, and Wang (【90†1993】) and Andrade, Chang, and Seasholes (【91†2008】), who derive price pressure predictions in equilibrium models. In their models, returns are positively related to contemporaneous order imbalances through an information effect and negatively related to lagged order imbalances through an inventory effect. Considering the effects of asymmetric information and inventory risk together, we estimate
$$$$\begin{align} \Delta s_{t}^{\text{post-L}} = \alpha + \beta _1 \text{OF}_{t}^{\text{pre}} + \beta _2 \text{OF}_{t}^{\text{post-L}}+\varepsilon _{t}, \end{align}$$$$(3)

where $$\Delta s_{t}^{\text{post-L}}$$ denotes the return measured over the postfix window on day t and OF$$_{t}^{\text{post-L}}$$ is the corresponding order flow. The order flow before the fix OF$$_{t}^{\text{pre}}$$ is measured (i) using the “pre-E” and the “E-L” window (labeled “pre-L”) as well as (ii) using the “pre-E” window only.

The results are summarized as follows. First, all coefficients on contemporaneous order flow in Table 【92†IX】 are strongly positive and highly significant, consistent with the idea that dealer order flow is informative about price discovery. Second, the coefficient on the lagged prefix order flow is always estimated to be negative and significant, consistent with conditional reversals arising around the fix due to inventory effects.

Interestingly, the relationship between prefix order flow and postfix returns remains statistically and economically strong if we exclude the last three hours leading up to the London fix and measure the order flow only up to the ECB fix. Thus, inventory effects are not simply driven by trading activity in the last few minutes leading up to the London fix as studied in previous literature (see, e.g., Evans (【26†2018】)).

### E. Liquidity Provision
In this section, we explore returns to liquidity provision and gauge whether dealers are indeed providing liquidity at the fixes.【94†20】

We start our analysis by considering a trader that seeks to exploit the intraday predictability around the European fixes. Expecting an appreciation of the U.S. dollar, they enter a position in the D2C market at $$t=1$$ and subsequently sell U.S. dollars at the fix ($$t=2$$). To also benefit from the postfix depreciation, they then reverse the trade and short the U.S. dollar, closing out the position at $$t=3$$.

Throughout, the trader always transacts in the D2C market and is always the liquidity demander, implying that they sell the foreign currency at the bid at $$t=1$$ and $$t=3$$. Most importantly, at the fix they buy the foreign currency at the ask, $$s_{2,D2C}^a$$ (equivalently, sell U.S. dollars at the bid). The resulting returns are the two legs of the reversal returns defined in equation (【95†A.1】) with transaction costs taken into account,
$$$$\begin{equation} \Delta s_{t,LD}^{\text{pre}} = s_{1,D2C}^b - s_{2,D2C}^a \quad \text{and} \quad \Delta s_{t,LD}^{\text{post}} = - s_{2,D2C}^a+ s_{3,D2C}^b, \end{equation}$$$$(4)
where the total return is calculated as the sum of the two legs.

In addition to the trader, we consider a dealer that acts as a liquidity provider in the D2C market and, on average, purchases foreign currencies for U.S. dollars at the fix to satisfy the unconditional demand for U.S. dollars. In contrast to a liquidity demander, however, liquidity providers purchase the foreign currency at the (lower) bid price. Furthermore, we assume that the dealer sources U.S. dollars in the D2D market in the morning ($$t=1$$).

To match the speculative positions of the trader, we assume that the dealer also reverses their position at the fix by shorting the U.S. dollar and closing out the position in the D2D market in a postfix trading period ($$t=3$$). Note that when sourcing U.S. dollars in the D2D market, the liquidity provider acts as the “aggressor” and sells foreign currency at the bid price $$s_{t,D2D}^b$$. The dealer buys the foreign currency at the bid (equivalently, sells U.S.
dollars at the ask) only when providing liquidity at the fix. The resulting returns for the liquidity provider and the two legs can be calculated as
$$$$\begin{equation} \Delta s_{t,LP}^{\text{pre}} = s_{1,D2D}^b - s_{2,D2C}^b \quad \text{and} \quad \Delta s_{t,LP}^{\text{post}} = - s_{2,D2C}^b+s_{3,D2D}^b, \end{equation}$$$$(5)
where the total return is again calculated as the sum of the two legs.

Table 【96†X】 reports unconditional returns for a liquidity demander and a liquidity provider as per equations (【97†4】) and (【98†5】). The results are summarized as follows. First, for the trader (or liquidity demander), reversal returns turn negative once transaction costs are taken into account. Thus, the unconditional return patterns cannot easily be arbitraged away by traders who seek to exploit the intraday reversals.

Second, and most importantly, returns to liquidity provision are positive, in line with the view that dealers supply dollars in exchange for a liquidity premium. The observation that both the prefix returns for liquidity provision are significantly positive is further consistent with a situation in which clients are demanding U.S. dollars ahead of the fixings and dealers raise their prices when streaming quotes. Indeed, if it were dealers demanding U.S.
dollar liquidity, one would expect the opposite finding, that is, negative returns for an unconditional trade in this direction.【99†21】

### F. Discussion

To summarize, we exploit data from both D2C and D2D platforms to present evidence consistent with an inventory risk explanation. We show that (i) unconditional demand for U.S. dollars occurs at the fix, (ii) return reversals are larger when order imbalances are bigger and in states of higher uncertainty, and (iii) expected returns to liquidity provision are substantial, providing indirect evidence that dealers do indeed act as liquidity providers to customers demanding U.S.
dollars, as opposed to demanding U.S. dollars that are sourced from their clients.

While the unconditional imbalance lines up with an unconditional V-shaped reversal pattern, our analysis is silent about the origin of this unconditional demand. However, we speculate that predictable demand for U.S. dollars at the fix could be related to the special role of the United States as the world's provider of safe assets and the dollar as the world's reserve currency (see, e.g., Jiang, Krishnamurthy, and Lustig (【100†2021】)).

We also note that predictable demand for immediacy at certain points within the day is consistent with existing evidence on intraday equity reversals (see, e.g., Heston, Korajczyk, and Sadka (【101†2010】) and Lou, Polk, and Skouras (【102†2019】)).
## VII. Conclusion

In this paper, we document a new stylized fact for intraday return patterns in currency markets: the U.S. dollar gradually appreciates ahead of the three major currency fixings and depreciates thereafter. That is, the U.S. dollar reaches an intraday peak at the Tokyo, ECB, and London fixes.

Using a set of natural experiments, we pin down the importance of published benchmark rates for the intraday reversal patterns. Furthermore, we show that the reversals around the fixes are a pervasive feature of the data, robust over the 21 years of our data span, and present for all of the G9 currencies, which cover close to 75% of global spot transaction volumes. The return patterns spill over into over-the-counter forward as well as exchange-traded futures markets.

This result is important for institutional investors and corporate hedgers alike, because it implies that the intraday timing of their speculative and hedging activities, as well as the timing of currency conversions and portfolio adjustments, affects their balance sheets.

We rule out a set of candidate explanations and provide evidence that is consistent with an explanation based on demand for immediacy combined with structural demand for U.S. dollars at the fixes. Using volume data from a D2D market, we document an unconditional order imbalance toward U.S. dollars ahead of the fixes. Reversal returns are increasing with higher order imbalance and higher uncertainty as proxied by FXV. Moreover, returns to liquidity provision can be substantial for dealers who source U.S.

dollars in the D2D market and act as liquidity providers at the fix. Finally, while an inventory management explanation is supported by the data, we leave the question of why there is a tilt toward prefix U.S. DD for future research.
